feed.title: Learning & Roadmaps — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: arxiv-sanity-lite
entry.summary: Karpathy's tool for searching, tagging and recommending arXiv papers; open source.

entry.title: Awesome Certificates
entry.summary: A list of free computer-science certificates you can add to your résumé. Unlike paid certificate programmes, it picks only free ones.

entry.title: Awesome Hackathon
entry.summary: A resource list for running fun and productive hackathons. Unlike participant guides, it focuses on the organiser’s side: planning, judging, tools and platforms.

entry.title: Awesome Product Management
entry.summary: A resource list for becoming a better product manager. Unlike general career lists, it gathers books, frameworks and tools specific to product management.

entry.title: Awesome Roadmaps
entry.summary: A list gathering clear roadmaps to improve your knowledge across fields.

entry.title: Awesome STEAM
entry.summary: Supplementary learning resources for science, technology, engineering, arts and maths. Unlike general learning lists, it uses the STEAM frame that includes the arts and focuses on school-level extras.

entry.title: Awesome Workshopper
entry.summary: A list of interactive command-line tutorials (workshoppers). Unlike browser-based tutorials, you solve exercises in the terminal with your own editor — the format NodeSchool uses.

entry.title: Awesome YouTubers
entry.summary: A list of quality YouTube channels that teach technology. Unlike a YouTube search, it hand-picks channels by topic.

entry.title: CSS Diner
entry.summary: A game teaching CSS selectors by picking dishes on a table. Unlike dry drills it turns selector syntax into a visual, fun puzzle.

entry.title: Distill
entry.summary: A research journal explaining machine-learning ideas through interactive visuals (on hiatus, but the archive is valuable).

entry.title: Duolingo
entry.summary: A platform teaching languages through gamified, short daily lessons.

entry.title: Flexbox Defense
entry.summary: A site teaching CSS Flexbox through a tower-defence game. Unlike the docs it fixes each alignment property with a game move.

entry.title: Full Stack Open
entry.summary: University of Helsinki's free, end-to-end full-stack course teaching React, Node and GraphQL.

entry.title: Learn to Code With Me
entry.summary: A resource gathering paths, tools and career advice for self-taught coders. Unlike single-topic sites it addresses “where to start and how to turn it into a job”.

entry.title: Silent Teacher
entry.summary: A game that teaches the basics of programming by trial and error, with no word of explanation. Unlike a lecture it has you discover the rule yourself.

entry.title: SoloLearn
entry.summary: A platform teaching programming on mobile through small lessons and community. Unlike long courses it is bite-sized enough to progress even on the bus.

entry.title: TechGuide
entry.summary: A site giving software’s different career paths (frontend, data, mobile) as visual roadmaps. Unlike a single resource it maps what to learn in which order for a role.

entry.title: 01 Edu Public
entry.summary: The open course-and-project repository of the 01 Edu school, built on a teacherless, peer-reviewed model. Unlike video courses it is project-based: with deliberately ambiguous tasks it teaches you to build your own solution.

entry.title: APMG International
entry.summary: An accreditation body running examinations for the AXELOS frameworks and others. Unlike the framework owners it is an independent examination institute — the same ITIL exam is available through several, and APMG is one of them.

entry.title: AXELOS
entry.summary: The owner of the ITIL, PRINCE2 and MSP frameworks. Unlike the security bodies it sits on the service and project management side — ITIL is the shared vocabulary of corporate IT, and security teams use the same terms for incident handling.

entry.title: BCS
entry.summary: The UK’s chartered professional body for IT, which certifies and also accredits university programmes. Unlike commercial examination institutes it is a professional institution, and a step on the path to chartered engineer status.

entry.title: CertNexus
entry.summary: A body issuing vendor-neutral certificates in emerging fields: cybersecurity, data science, AI and IoT. Its difference from the established organisations is that focus — a yardstick in areas the traditional catalogues have not caught up with.

entry.title: CompTIA
entry.summary: The standard entry rung through Security+, Network+ and A+. Unlike senior certifications it demands no prior experience, which is why it appears in first-job listings and in the US defence sector’s DoD 8570 list. Do not expect depth.

entry.title: EXIN
entry.summary: A Dutch vendor-neutral examination institute certifying in information security management (ISO 27001) and data protection. Unlike training providers it only examines: where you learned the material is not its concern.

entry.title: GAQM
entry.summary: A body issuing vendor-neutral certificates across a wide field — project management, quality, security. Against the established organisations it is cheap with flexible entry requirements; in exchange, employer recognition is limited.

entry.title: PECB
entry.summary: A body certifying auditors and implementers against ISO standards including 27001, 22301 and 9001. Against EXIN it operates through an accredited trainer network and confers lead auditor status.

entry.title: PMI
entry.summary: The body behind PMP, project management’s most widespread certification. Against PRINCE2 it is built on knowledge areas rather than a process template, and it requires experience: documented project hours are needed to apply.

entry.title: Scrum.org
entry.summary: The certification body founded by Ken Schwaber, one of Scrum’s originators. Against Scrum Alliance you can sit the exam without taking a course, and the certificate carries no renewal fee — pass once and it stands.

entry.title: SECO-Institute
entry.summary: A European body certifying security roles along a tiered path. Unlike organisations selling individual exams it defines role-based tracks — which certificate comes in which order, from analyst to architect.

entry.title: Algorithm Visualizer
entry.summary: A platform that visualises an algorithm step by step alongside its code, and runs code you write yourself. That is the difference from a canned animation: you can change the algorithm and watch what happens.

entry.title: Teach Yourself CS
entry.summary: Nine subjects for self-teaching computer science, each with exactly one book and one course recommended. Unlike other roadmaps it refuses to offer options: it settles the "which resource" argument for you and explains why it chose that one.

entry.title: Kodluyoruz
entry.summary: A Turkish social enterprise offering free software training. Unlike paid bootcamps, it removes the cost barrier and aims to connect graduates to jobs.

entry.title: 1000 Projects
entry.summary: A very broad compilation of project ideas — high on quantity, with the filtering left to you.

entry.title: App Ideas
entry.summary: App ideas graded by difficulty, each with user stories and bonus features written out. That level of specification is what separates it from plain project lists.

entry.title: Awesome CS Courses
entry.summary: A list of university computer science courses published online, focused on those whose lecture notes and assignments are open. Unlike MOOC platforms, it links straight to the universities’ own course pages.

entry.title: Boot.dev
entry.summary: A backend-focused curriculum with in-browser exercises. Unlike general bootcamps it looks only at the server side.

entry.title: Class Central
entry.summary: A search index across Coursera, edX and dozens more, letting you line up different universities’ versions of the same subject side by side.

entry.title: Classpert
entry.summary: A directory searching online courses across platforms. Against checking each platform it compares price and length — five courses on the same subject, side by side.

entry.title: Computerphile
entry.summary: A channel explaining computer science concepts in conversation with academics. Unlike tutorial channels it does not teach code — it explains the idea behind encryption, compilers or complexity.

entry.title: CrashCourse
entry.summary: Fast, animated short courses on many subjects from computer science to history.
